Ceramic thermal barrier coatings were investigated at NASA Lewis under the DOE-sponsored Critical Research and Advanced Technology Support Project.
In early burner rig tests, the zirconia-yttria/nickel-chromium-aluminum-yttrium coating system was found to be sensitive to sodium and vanadium concentrations in the fuel.
The locations of coating spallation corresponded to areas where combustion products were predicted to condense.
Three new thermal barrier coating systems were identified: calcium silicate, ZrO2-8w/oY203, and a MgO-NiCrAlY cermet.
Reducing the ceramic layer thickness from 0.038 to 0.013 cm increased the spall resistance of the thermal barrier coatings.
Using more oxidation/corrosion resistant bond coats also improved the spall resistance of the thermal barrier coatings.

Bond coats with higher Cr and Al content, as well as increased coating thickness, arc power, and hydrogen in the arc gas, significantly improved the oxidation resistance and thermal barrier coating life.
The calcium silicate coating survived over 600 one-hour cycles before spalling, compared to about 60 cycles for the baseline zirconia-yttria/NiCrAlY system.
The MgO-NiCrAlY cermet coating survived 1000 one-hour cycles without spalling, but experienced about 50% thickness reduction due to erosion or microspalling.
Reducing the ceramic coating thickness from 0.038 to 0.013 cm extended the life of calcium silicate and ZrO2-8w/oY203 thermal barrier coatings by about 4 times.
High Cr + Al and Co-based bond coats improved the durability of calcium silicate and ZrO2-8w/oY203 thermal barrier coatings by 2 to 3 times.
Condensation and penetration of Na, V, and Co-containing combustion products, as well as CaSO4 formation and phase changes, were found to contribute to the failure of the calcium silicate coatings.
Thermochemical calculations of condensate dew points and melting points, combined with temperature profiles, provided a good explanation for the observed coating failure locations.
Reaction studies between ceramic coating materials and potential air, fuel, and bond coat impurities provided additional understanding of coating failure mechanisms.

The DOE-sponsored Critical Research and Advanced Technology Support Project at NASA Lewis made substantial progress in understanding thermal barrier coating behavior and improving their durability for industrial/utility gas turbine applications.
